newsitem.title: USA: Crude oil rises, coffee higher in volatile trade.
newsitem.headline: Crude oil rises, coffee higher in volatile trade.

text.p: Crude oil prices rose Wednesday on Mideast tensions, and coffee ended a volatile day higher on worries about Colombia's supplies.
Grain prices fell but gains in copper, cocoa and pork bellies helped the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures contracts close 1.27 points higher at 242.89.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for April delivery settled up 11 cents at $21.11 a barrel after a Kurdish group in Iraq said rival Kurds and Iraqi forces were preparing for an attack against it.

The Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) said there were signs of an imminent attack by the rival Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) of Massoud Barzani and troops of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein on the PUK's stronghold, Sulaimaniya province. The KDP dismissed the PUK claim.

Iraq has an agreement with the United Nations to export oil in exchange for humanitarian aid. The PUK's statements created concern that a possible attack by Iraqi troops on the PUK could lead to the suspension of the U.N. pact and tighten crude supplies.

"It may have some sort of basis in fact, but whether it leads to anything unusual in Iraq and affects supply is another story," said Tim Evans, analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group. "The market decided it's worth a little more than 10 cents, and that seems about right.
March heating oil ended 0.14 cent a gallon lower at 56.68 cents. March gasoline ended 0.03 cent higher at 62.26 cents.
At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee futures ended higher in volatile trading.

Prices came reeling off the day's highs, however, in late trading when a spokesman for Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation said a crop estimate of 8.3 million bags he had released earlier was erroneous.

"The calculation was wrong," said Roman Medina, explaining that he failed to take into account 2 million bags of production from January to March. He said production for the 1996-97 coffee year was still seen at 10.4 million 132-pound bags, down from 12.9 million last year.

May coffee futures soared to fresh life-of-contract highs of 177.00 cents per pound on the 8.3-million-bag forecast. May coffee ended at 172.85 cents, up 9.60 cents, after falling back as low as 165.60 cents on Medina's corrected estimate.
"The market is definitely worried about tight supplies," said analyst Ann Prendergast. "And this (Colombian news) is keeping that fear raw."
May cocoa closed at a two-week high, up $23 at $1,302 per metric ton.
With world supply expected to show a shortfall of around 200,000 tons in the current crop year after a surplus a year earlier, cocoa may post further gains, Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka said.
"Cocoa is acting much better," Spilka said. "The market is extremely undervalued. There is plenty of cocoa around now, but that won't be the case in the coming weeks."

Copper prices ended sharply higher, with the market at its strongest since just before the Sumitomo copper trading scandal broke in June 1996. March copper on the Comex division of Nymex ended 3.40 cents higher at 114.85 cents per pound.
"It may go a little bit higher, but we will have to see some Chinese demand or unexpected supply disruptions to continue with this type of trend," said David Rinehimer of Smith Barney.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, sales of soybean futures by commercial grain firms in the United States and overseas to cash in on high prices pressured prices. March soybeans ended 7-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $7.83-3/4.
March wheat closed 6-1/4 cents lower at $3.70-3/4 a bushel, and March corn down 1/2 cent at $2.92-3/4 a bushel.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, March pork belly futures closed up a strong 2.125 cents at 79.150 cents, fuelled in part by talk that a possible price war by fast-food chains led by McDonald's might include more bacon in hamburgers.

"We have an abundance of the lower grade-type beef (used for hamburgers) and it will help bacon to some degree because it is on some of those sandwiches," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
